claim: InSyn1 (Inhibitory Synaptic protein 1) is a critical component of the dystroglycan complex (DGC).
source: Here, we report Inhibitory Synaptic protein 1 (InSyn1) is a critical component of the DGC whose loss alters the composition of the GABAergic synapses, excitatory/inhibitory balance in vitro and in vivo, and cognitive behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Loss of InSyn1 alters the composition of GABAergic synapses.
source: Here, we report Inhibitory Synaptic protein 1 (InSyn1) is a critical component of the DGC whose loss alters the composition of the GABAergic synapses, excitatory/inhibitory balance in vitro and in vivo, and cognitive behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Loss of InSyn1 alters excitatory/inhibitory balance in vitro and in vivo.
source: Here, we report Inhibitory Synaptic protein 1 (InSyn1) is a critical component of the DGC whose loss alters the composition of the GABAergic synapses, excitatory/inhibitory balance in vitro and in vivo, and cognitive behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by MEA recordings and in vivo calcium imaging data.

claim: Loss of InSyn1 affects cognitive behavior.
source: Here, we report Inhibitory Synaptic protein 1 (InSyn1) is a critical component of the DGC whose loss alters the composition of the GABAergic synapses, excitatory/inhibitory balance in vitro and in vivo, and cognitive behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral testing data including fear conditioning.

claim: Association of InSyn1 with DGC subunits is required for InSyn1 synaptic localization.
source: Association of InSyn1 with DGC subunits is required for InSyn1 synaptic localization.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by CRISPR depletion and structure-function experiments.

claim: InSyn1 null neurons show a significant reduction in DGC distribution.
source: InSyn1 null neurons also show a significant reduction in DGC and GABA receptor distribution as well as abnormal neuronal network activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunostaining quantification data in Figure 4.

claim: InSyn1 null neurons show a significant reduction in GABA receptor distribution.
source: InSyn1 null neurons also show a significant reduction in DGC and GABA receptor distribution as well as abnormal neuronal network activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunostaining quantification data in Figure 5.

claim: InSyn1 null neurons show abnormal neuronal network activity.
source: InSyn1 null neurons also show a significant reduction in DGC and GABA receptor distribution as well as abnormal neuronal network activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by MEA recording data in Figure 6.

claim: InSyn1 null mice exhibit elevated neuronal firing patterns in the hippocampus.
source: Moreover, InSyn1 null mice exhibit elevated neuronal firing patterns in the hippocampus and deficits in fear conditioning memory.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in vivo calcium imaging data in Figure 8.

claim: InSyn1 null mice exhibit deficits in fear conditioning memory.
source: Moreover, InSyn1 null mice exhibit elevated neuronal firing patterns in the hippocampus and deficits in fear conditioning memory.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figure 9.

claim: Human mutations in the dystroglycan complex (DGC) result in muscular dystrophy.
source: Human mutations in the dystroglycan complex (DGC) result in not only muscular dystrophy but also cognitive impairments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: Human mutations in the dystroglycan complex (DGC) result in cognitive impairments.
source: Human mutations in the dystroglycan complex (DGC) result in not only muscular dystrophy but also cognitive impairments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: GABA-mediated inhibitory synaptic transmission is fundamental to almost all aspects of brain function.
source: GABA-mediated inhibitory synaptic-transmission is fundamental to almost all aspects of brain function and its dysregulation is thought to contribute to many neurological disorders including epilepsy, intellectual disability, autism and schizophrenia (Marín, 2012; Zoghbi and Bear, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Dysregulation of GABA-mediated inhibitory synaptic transmission contributes to epilepsy, intellectual disability, autism and schizophrenia.
source: GABA-mediated inhibitory synaptic-transmission is fundamental to almost all aspects of brain function and its dysregulation is thought to contribute to many neurological disorders including epilepsy, intellectual disability, autism and schizophrenia (Marín, 2012; Zoghbi and Bear, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Postsynaptic GABAARs mediating phasic inhibition consist of two α1, α2, or α3 subunits with two β2 or β3 subunits, and a single γ2 subunit.
source: Postsynaptic GABAARs mediating phasic inhibition consist of two α1, α2, or α3 subunits with two β2 or β3 subunits, and a single γ2 subunit (Olsen and Sieghart, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The dystrophin/dystroglycan complex (DGC) physically bridges the extracellular matrix and the actin cytoskeleton.
source: The dystrophin/dystroglycan complex (DGC) is better known for its importance for the integrity of muscle fibers against mechanical stress by physically bridging the extracellular matrix and the actin cytoskeleton (Allikian and McNally, 2007; O'Brien and Kunkel, 2001; Sunada and Campbell, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Muscular dystrophies are often associated with cognitive deficits, epilepsy and other neurological disorders.
source: However, muscular dystrophies, which are caused by gene mutations encoding this protein complex, are often associated with cognitive deficits, epilepsy and other neurological disorders, highlighting its importance in the nervous system (Godfrey et al., 2011; Hendriksen and Vles, 2008; Waite et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In neurons, DGC forms a complex with α-, β-dystroglycan, dystrophin and distinct isoforms of dystrobrevin and syntrophin.
source: In neurons, DGC forms a complex with α-, β-dystroglycan, dystrophin and distinct isoforms of dystrobrevin and syntrophin.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: DGC components co-localize with a subset of inhibitory synapses in distinct brain regions.
source: They co-localize with a subset of inhibitory synapses in distinct brain regions and are important for targeting and modulating GABAA receptors (Côté et al., 2002; Knuesel et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: DGC components are important for targeting and modulating GABAA receptors.
source: They co-localize with a subset of inhibitory synapses in distinct brain regions and are important for targeting and modulating GABAA receptors (Côté et al., 2002; Knuesel et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Dystroglycan and its glycosylation may be crucial for the expression of homeostatic synaptic plasticity at GABAergic synapses.
source: Dystroglycan and its glycosylation may be crucial for the expression of homeostatic synaptic plasticity at GABAergic synapses (Pribiag et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: InSyn1 was identified as one of the abundant previously uncharacterized proteins in the iPSD proteome dataset.
source: InSyn1 was one of the abundant previously uncharacterized proteins (Human: UPF0583 protein C15orf59, Mouse: 6030419C18Rik) in our iPSD proteome dataset, and we found it is functionally important for synaptic inhibition both at the single-cell and at the network level (Uezu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: InSyn1 is functionally important for synaptic inhibition at the single-cell level.
source: InSyn1 was one of the abundant previously uncharacterized proteins (Human: UPF0583 protein C15orf59, Mouse: 6030419C18Rik) in our iPSD proteome dataset, and we found it is functionally important for synaptic inhibition both at the single-cell and at the network level (Uezu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: InSyn1 is functionally important for synaptic inhibition at the network level.
source: InSyn1 was one of the abundant previously uncharacterized proteins (Human: UPF0583 protein C15orf59, Mouse: 6030419C18Rik) in our iPSD proteome dataset, and we found it is functionally important for synaptic inhibition both at the single-cell and at the network level (Uezu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: InSyn1 was highly co-localized with gephyrin and αDG.
source: Previously we demonstrated that InSyn1 was enriched in the iPSD and that it was highly co-localized with the markers of inhibitory synapses gephyrin and αDG, which both serve to scaffold and organize the iPSD (Uezu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: Gephyrin and αDG serve to scaffold and organize the iPSD.
source: Previously we demonstrated that InSyn1 was enriched in the iPSD and that it was highly co-localized with the markers of inhibitory synapses gephyrin and αDG, which both serve to scaffold and organize the iPSD (Uezu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: CRISPR-mediated depletion of gephyrin decreased gephyrin cluster density by 81% compared to control.
source: Depletion of endogenous protein levels of gephyrin or αDG was confirmed by immunostaining of both proteins, demonstrating the density of gephyrin or αDG clusters was decreased by 81% and 89% compared to negative control (empty sgRNA) samples (Figure 1A), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantification shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CRISPR-mediated depletion of αDG decreased αDG cluster density by 89% compared to control.
source: Depletion of endogenous protein levels of gephyrin or αDG was confirmed by immunostaining of both proteins, demonstrating the density of gephyrin or αDG clusters was decreased by 81% and 89% compared to negative control (empty sgRNA) samples (Figure 1A), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantification shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CRISPR-mediated gephyrin depletion did not alter the distribution of InSyn1 puncta.
source: CRISPR-mediated gephyrin depletion did not alter the distribution of InSyn1 puncta.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by imaging and quantification in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Following αDG depletion, InSyn1 dramatically diminished its clustering and was diffuse throughout the soma and dendrites.
source: However, following αDG depletion, InSyn1 dramatically diminished its clustering and was diffuse throughout the soma and dendrites (Figure 1B; bottom panels).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by imaging shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Endogenous InSyn1 localization is αDG dependent.
source: To further evaluate whether endogenous InSyn1 localization is also αDG dependent, we took advantage of Homology-Independent Targeted Integration (HITI) method to label C-terminus of InSyn1 with a highly antigenic spaghetti-monster tag (smFP-HA) in Cas9 KI neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Suzuki et al., 2016; Viswanathan et al., 2015). We found a dramatic reduction of endogenous InSyn1-labeled neurons in CRISPR depleted αDG samples but no difference in gephyrin depletion compared to control (Fig. D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by HITI labeling data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The first 60 amino acids region of InSyn1 harbors a predicted coiled-coil sequence.
source: InSyn1 is a 292 amino acid protein and the only potential structural insight available is that the first 60 amino acids region harbors a predicted coiled-coil sequence, which often mediates protein-protein interactions (Burkhard et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Coiled-coil sequences often mediate protein-protein interactions.
source: InSyn1 is a 292 amino acid protein and the only potential structural insight available is that the first 60 amino acids region harbors a predicted coiled-coil sequence, which often mediates protein-protein interactions (Burkhard et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Full-length InSyn1-GFP exhibited puncta staining that strongly colocalized with αDG.
source: Full-length InSyn1-GFP, as well as truncation mutants of the C-terminus or middle portions of the protein exhibited puncta staining that strongly colocalized with αDG.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by imaging in Figure 2B.

claim: InSyn1 truncation mutants of the C-terminus exhibited puncta staining that strongly colocalized with αDG.
source: Full-length InSyn1-GFP, as well as truncation mutants of the C-terminus or middle portions of the protein exhibited puncta staining that strongly colocalized with αDG.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by imaging in Figure 2B-C.

claim: InSyn1 truncation mutants of the middle portions exhibited puncta staining that strongly colocalized with αDG.
source: Full-length InSyn1-GFP, as well as truncation mutants of the C-terminus or middle portions of the protein exhibited puncta staining that strongly colocalized with αDG.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by imaging in Figure 2B-C.

claim: An N-terminal truncated version of InSyn1 (InSyn1ΔN-GFP) showed diffuse expression throughout the neurons.
source: In contrast, an N-terminal truncated version, InSyn1ΔN-GFP, showed diffuse expression throughout the neurons (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by imaging in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Loss of the N-terminal region (a.a. 1–60) of InSyn1 disrupted its localization in neurons.
source: Quantitative analysis, comparing the distribution index of each InSyn1 deletion mutant to soluble GFP, confirmed the loss of the N-terminal region (a.a. 1–60) disrupted its localization in neurons (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantification in Figure 2C.

claim: α1-syntrophin functions as a docking site for various proteins through its PDZ and PH domains.
source: α1-syntrophin is known to function as a docking site for various proteins through its PDZ and PH domains, including ion channels, GPCRs, water channels, kinases and phosphatases in the nervous system (Brenman et al., 1996; Connors et al., 2004; Neely et al., 2001), while the C-terminal SU domain mediates its interaction with dystrophin and utrophin (Kramarcy et al., 1994; Yang et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The C-terminal SU domain of α1-syntrophin mediates its interaction with dystrophin and utrophin.
source: α1-syntrophin is known to function as a docking site for various proteins through its PDZ and PH domains, including ion channels, GPCRs, water channels, kinases and phosphatases in the nervous system (Brenman et al., 1996; Connors et al., 2004; Neely et al., 2001), while the C-terminal SU domain mediates its interaction with dystrophin and utrophin (Kramarcy et al., 1994; Yang et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Dystrobrevins interact with dystrophin and syntrophin.
source: Dystrobrevins are an integral component of DGC that interact with dystrophin and syntrophin as well as other signaling proteins, such as dysbindin, Kif5, and the regulatory subunit of PKA (Benson et al., 2001; Ceccarini et al., 2007; Macioce, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Dystrobrevins interact with dysbindin, Kif5, and the regulatory subunit of PKA.
source: Dystrobrevins are an integral component of DGC that interact with dystrophin and syntrophin as well as other signaling proteins, such as dysbindin, Kif5, and the regulatory subunit of PKA (Benson et al., 2001; Ceccarini et al., 2007; Macioce, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Mice lacking both α and β-dystrobrevin show defects in inhibitory synaptic structure and motor functions.
source: Mice lacking both α and β-dystrobrevin show defects in inhibitory synaptic structure and motor functions, suggesting their important roles in organizing the DGC at the CNS (Grady, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Full-length InSyn1 bound to α1-syntrophin and β-dystrobrevin.
source: Interestingly, we found that while full-length InSyn1 bound to α1-syntrophin and β-dystrobrevin, only the N-terminus deletion of InSyn1 (InSyn1ΔN) disrupted the interaction with both α1-syntrophin and β-dystrobrevin (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by co-IP data in Figure 2E.

claim: The N-terminus deletion of InSyn1 (InSyn1ΔN) disrupted the interaction with α1-syntrophin.
source: Interestingly, we found that while full-length InSyn1 bound to α1-syntrophin and β-dystrobrevin, only the N-terminus deletion of InSyn1 (InSyn1ΔN) disrupted the interaction with both α1-syntrophin and β-dystrobrevin (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by co-IP data in Figure 2E.

claim: The N-terminus deletion of InSyn1 (InSyn1ΔN) disrupted the interaction with β-dystrobrevin.
source: Interestingly, we found that while full-length InSyn1 bound to α1-syntrophin and β-dystrobrevin, only the N-terminus deletion of InSyn1 (InSyn1ΔN) disrupted the interaction with both α1-syntrophin and β-dystrobrevin (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by co-IP data in Figure 2E.

claim: None of the InSyn1 deletion mutants disrupted the interaction with gephyrin.
source: We also assessed the interaction between these InSyn1 mutants and gephyrin and found none of the deletion mutants disrupted this interaction, suggesting multiple regions of InSyn1 are involved in the interactions with gephyrin and that truncation of the N-terminus did not generally disrupt all functions of InSyn1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by co-IP data in Figure 2E.

claim: Multiple regions of InSyn1 are involved in the interactions with gephyrin.
source: We also assessed the interaction between these InSyn1 mutants and gephyrin and found none of the deletion mutants disrupted this interaction, suggesting multiple regions of InSyn1 are involved in the interactions with gephyrin and that truncation of the N-terminus did not generally disrupt all functions of InSyn1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data showing that no single deletion disrupted gephyrin binding.

claim: InSyn1 associates with the DGC complex via its N-terminal predicted coiled-coil region.
source: These results demonstrate that InSyn1 associates with the DGC complex via its N-terminal predicted coiled-coil region and that this interaction is required for its proper localization in neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the structure-function and co-IP experiments.

claim: The interaction of InSyn1 with the DGC via its N-terminal region is required for its proper localization in neurons.
source: These results demonstrate that InSyn1 associates with the DGC complex via its N-terminal predicted coiled-coil region and that this interaction is required for its proper localization in neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the structure-function and co-IP experiments.

claim: Insyn1 mRNAs were detected throughout the mouse brain.
source: Insyn1 mRNAs were detected throughout the mouse brain, with high expression in the hippocampus, olfactory bulb, cerebellum and modest expression in the cortex, thalamus, midbrain, and pons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by PLISH imaging in Figure 3A.

claim: Insyn1 shows high expression in the hippocampus, olfactory bulb, and cerebellum.
source: Insyn1 mRNAs were detected throughout the mouse brain, with high expression in the hippocampus, olfactory bulb, cerebellum and modest expression in the cortex, thalamus, midbrain, and pons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by PLISH imaging in Figure 3A.

claim: Insyn1 shows modest expression in the cortex, thalamus, midbrain, and pons.
source: Insyn1 mRNAs were detected throughout the mouse brain, with high expression in the hippocampus, olfactory bulb, cerebellum and modest expression in the cortex, thalamus, midbrain, and pons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by PLISH imaging in Figure 3A.

claim: InSyn1 was robustly expressed in the granule cell layer of the dentate gyrus (DG).
source: In the hippocampus, InSyn1 was robustly expressed in the granule cell layer of the dentate gyrus (DG) and other pyramidal cell layer regions such as CA1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by PLISH imaging in Figure 3B.

claim: InSyn1 was robustly expressed in pyramidal cell layer regions such as CA1.
source: In the hippocampus, InSyn1 was robustly expressed in the granule cell layer of the dentate gyrus (DG) and other pyramidal cell layer regions such as CA1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by PLISH imaging in Figure 3B.

claim: Insyn1 expression was detected in all cells within the hilus.
source: Insyn1 expression was detected in all cells within the hilus, suggesting InSyn1 may be expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by PLISH imaging.

claim: InSyn1 may be expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: Insyn1 expression was detected in all cells within the hilus, suggesting InSyn1 may be expressed in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Insyn1 is expressed in all hilar cells, which include both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.

claim: Strong Insyn1 expression was observed in Purkinje cells in the cerebellum.
source: In the cerebellum, we observed strong expression of Insyn1 in Purkinje cells (PC), whereas comparatively weaker expression was detected in the internal granule cell layer (IGL).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by PLISH imaging in Figure 3B.

claim: Weaker Insyn1 expression was detected in the internal granule cell layer (IGL) of the cerebellum.
source: In the cerebellum, we observed strong expression of Insyn1 in Purkinje cells (PC), whereas comparatively weaker expression was detected in the internal granule cell layer (IGL).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by PLISH imaging in Figure 3B.

claim: InSyn1 KO mice harbor an 11-basepair missense deletion causing an out-of-frame mutation following 34 amino-acids and a premature stop codon.
source: This resulted in mice harboring an 11-basepair missense deletion causing an out-of-frame mutation following 34 amino-acids and a premature stop codon in a highly conserved region of InSyn1 including predicted coiled-coil region (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by sequencing data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: InSyn1 protein expression was lost in Insyn1-/- neurons.
source: However, InSyn1 expression was abolished in Insyn1-/- neurons confirming InSyn1 protein expression was lost following the disruptive deletion in Exon 2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by HITI labeling data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Loss of InSyn1 significantly impacted the density and clustering of αDG.
source: Loss of InSyn1 significantly impacted the density and clustering of αDG (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The density of αDG clustering was decreased by 41% in the neurite regions of InSyn1 KO neurons compared to WT neurons.
source: We found that compared to WT neurons, the density of αDG clustering was decreased by 41% in the neurite regions (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantification in Figure 4B.

claim: There is an apparent increase in αDG cluster area in both neurite regions (30%) and perisomatic regions (18%) in InSyn1 KO neurons.
source: In contrast, analyzing the αDG cluster area demonstrated that there is an apparent increase in both regions (neurite regions; 30%, perisomatic regions; 18%) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantification in Figure 4B.

claim: The total αDG cluster area did not show a difference between WT and InSyn1 KO neurons.
source: The total αDG cluster area did not show a difference between WT and InSyn1 KO neurons, suggesting the overall expression of αDG has not changed and is instead re-distributed to the fewer remaining αDG clusters in the KO neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The overall expression of αDG has not changed in InSyn1 KO neurons and is instead re-distributed to the fewer remaining αDG clusters.
source: The total αDG cluster area did not show a difference between WT and InSyn1 KO neurons, suggesting the overall expression of αDG has not changed and is instead re-distributed to the fewer remaining αDG clusters in the KO neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that total αDG cluster area is unchanged despite changes in density and individual cluster size.

claim: Dystrophin showed a region-specific reduction of puncta density in InSyn1 KO neurons.
source: Furthermore, another DGC component dystrophin showed a similar region-specific reduction of puncta density in KO neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: InSyn1 regulates the spatial distribution of αDG.
source: Together, these data demonstrate InSyn1 regulates the spatial distribution of αDG and that its loss results in a corresponding alteration across αDG-positive synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the αDG clustering analysis.

claim: Loss of InSyn1 results in a corresponding alteration across αDG-positive synapses.
source: Together, these data demonstrate InSyn1 regulates the spatial distribution of αDG and that its loss results in a corresponding alteration across αDG-positive synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the αDG clustering analysis.

claim: There was no significant change in the density or the cluster size of gephyrin between WT and InSyn1 KO neurons in both neurite and perisomatic regions.
source: We also performed the same analysis of gephyrin following the loss of InSyn1 (Figure 4C). Consistent with our in vitro findings, there was no significant change in the density or the cluster size of gephyrin between WT and KO neurons both in neurite and perisomatic regions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 4C-D.

claim: There was no significant change in the cluster density of GABAARα1 in either perisomatic or neurite regions in InSyn1 KO neurons compared to WT.
source: In InSyn1 KO neurons, there was no significant change in the cluster density of GABAARα1 in either region compared to WT (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantification in Figure 5B.

claim: There were no significant changes in the expression of GABAARβ3 in InSyn1 KO neurons.
source: We also found no significant changes in the expression of β3, which is an important subunit in inhibitory transmission in the hippocampus CA1 regions (Nguyen and Nicoll, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantification in Figure 5B.

claim: There was a marked reduction of GABAARα2 cluster density in the perisomatic (32%) and neurite (43%) regions in InSyn1 KO neurons.
source: However, we found a marked reduction of α2 cluster density in the perisomatic (32%) and neurite (43%) regions.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantification in Figure 5B.

claim: GABAARγ2 showed a 28% reduction of cluster density in the perisomatic region in InSyn1 KO neurons.
source: In the perisomatic region, γ2 showed a 28% reduction of cluster density, consistent with our previous CRISPR-dependent acute depletion (Uezu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantification in Figure 5B.

claim: There was a reduction in the area of GABAARα2 and β3 clusters in the neurite regions in InSyn1 KO neurons.
source: There was also a reduction in the area of α2 and β3 clusters in the neurite regions (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantification in Figure 5B.

claim: αDG staining was positive only in a subset of hippocampal neurons.
source: We have noticed that αDG staining was positive only in a subset of hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an observation from immunostaining experiments.

claim: DGC localizes in a subset of the inhibitory synapses.
source: Additionally, it is known that DGC localizes in a subset of the inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as established knowledge.

claim: The DGC exists only in a fraction of gephyrin-positive synapses.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown that the DGC exists only in a fraction of gephyrin-positive synapses by co-staining with βDG and gephyrin (Lévi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: There was a decrease of GABAARα2 subunit cluster density in the neurite region in αDG negative InSyn1 KO neurons.
source: Based on this information, we sought to analyze only αDG negative neurons that should mainly express gephyrin. After applying the same analysis method, we found a decrease of α2 subunit cluster density in the neurite region (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: InSyn1 has a subunit-specific effect on GABAARs distribution in hippocampal neurons.
source: Together, these data show that InSyn1 has a subunit-specific effect on GABAARs distribution in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the GABAAR subunit analysis.

claim: InSyn1 null hippocampal neurons exhibit a significant alteration in DGC composition at inhibitory synapses.
source: Furthermore, InSyn1 null hippocampal neurons exhibit a significant alteration in DGC and GABAAR composition at inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: InSyn1 null hippocampal neurons exhibit a significant alteration in GABAAR composition at inhibitory synapses.
source: Furthermore, InSyn1 null hippocampal neurons exhibit a significant alteration in DGC and GABAAR composition at inhibitory synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Cultured cortical neurons begin with random neuronal firing, which gradually exhibits network activity characterized by increasing spike firing rate, long bursting activity, and global synchronization.
source: Cultured cortical neurons begin with random neuronal firing, which gradually exhibits network activity characterized by increasing spike firing rate, long bursting activity, and global synchronization that indicate the maturation of neuronal connectivity (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as established knowledge about neuronal development in culture.

claim: There was an increase in the mean spontaneous firing rate of InSyn1 null neurons compared to WT at DIV8 and DIV11.
source: We found an increase in the mean spontaneous and evoked firing rate of InSyn1 null neurons compared to WT at DIV8 and DIV11, but no difference at DIV14 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) as well as no differences in network synchrony (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by MEA data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There was an increase in the mean evoked firing rate of InSyn1 null neurons compared to WT at DIV8 and DIV11.
source: We found an increase in the mean spontaneous and evoked firing rate of InSyn1 null neurons compared to WT at DIV8 and DIV11, but no difference at DIV14 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) as well as no differences in network synchrony (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by MEA data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There was no difference in firing rate between WT and InSyn1 null neurons at DIV14.
source: We found an increase in the mean spontaneous and evoked firing rate of InSyn1 null neurons compared to WT at DIV8 and DIV11, but no difference at DIV14 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) as well as no differences in network synchrony (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by MEA data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There were no differences in network synchrony between WT and InSyn1 null neurons.
